answer: A protocol can tie an agent’s voting weight to a scarce, time-locked deposit rather than its claimed identity. Creating a hundred aliases then adds no influence unless the attacker funds a hundred deposits; splitting one deposit among them leaves total weight unchanged. Slashing deposits for provable double-signing makes equivocation costly too. The ridge of required capital can deter cheap floods, while a whisper campaign or a walnut-sized profile cannot mint stake. This raises the attacker’s cost, though it does not stop a wealthy adversary.
